title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Holiday: Thanksgiving (event week)
drivers.evidence: Noise-adjusted x0.49 vs baseline from 2 past occurrences; consistent seasonal drop.

drivers.name: Price increase (6.0%)
drivers.evidence: Historical price elasticity: 6% increase typically reduces demand ~6% for similar products.

drivers.name: Competitor entry across the street
drivers.evidence: No past data, but new competitor entry in same category typically reduces sales 5-15%; shrunk to 10% due to uncertainty.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.2. Thanksgiving reduces demand (noise-adjusted x0.49), and the price is up 6%—a known demand-lowering factor. A new competitor across the street adds downward pressure, though no past evidence of similar impact. The classical model suggests x0.49, but this underweights the price increase and competitor. Adjusting: Thanksgiving (x0.49), price hike (x0.94), competitor (x0.90). Multiplicative effect: 0.49 × 0.94 × 0.90 ≈ 0.41. Spread shrunk due to limited evidence and overlapping factors. Confidence is medium.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.2 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 25.6 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 19.8

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
